purpose: An electrically operated switch with total galvanic isolation. A tiny 5V signal from the Arduino safely turns on and off high-voltage, high-current AC or DC devices without any electrical connection between the logic and power circuits.

whenToUse.scenario: Switching AC Mains Appliances (Lamps, Fans, Heaters)
whenToUse.why: Microcontroller pins cannot touch 110V/230V AC without instant catastrophic destruction. Relays use an air gap and optocoupler to keep lethal mains voltages completely isolated from the Arduino.
whenToUse.recommended: Songle SRD-05VDC-SL-C (Mechanical) or Fotek / Omron (Solid State Relay)

whenToUse.scenario: High-Current DC Loads (12V/24V Pumps, Solenoid Valves, Car Accessories)
whenToUse.why: Loads drawing 3A to 10A would melt an Arduino GPIO pin (max 20 mA). Mechanical relays easily handle up to 10A continuous DC.
When an alarm or cooling fan must stay running even if the Arduino loses power or crashes, wiring to the NC terminal guarantees power stays connected until actively broken.
whenToUse.recommended: Mechanical Relay using COM and NC contacts

whenToUse.scenario: Frequent, Silent Switching (Solid State Relay / SSR)
whenToUse.why: Mechanical relays click loudly and wear out after ~100 000 operations. Solid State Relays (SSR) have zero moving parts, are 100% silent, and switch in under 1 millisecond.
whenToUse.recommended: SSR-25DA (for high AC loads) or Omron G3MB-202P

basics.title: What a relay does
basics.text: An electrically operated mechanical or electronic switch. A low-power 5V control signal from an Arduino pin (which can supply only ~20 mA) safely switches high-power devices like 12V motors, water valves, lamps, or solenoids.

basics.title: Galvanic isolation
basics.text: The coil circuit connected to your Arduino is physically and magnetically isolated from the high-voltage load contacts. Power surges, motor inductive kicks, or shorts in the load cannot reach the microcontroller.

basics.title: Active-LOW triggers
basics.text: Most 5V Arduino relay modules use an active-LOW optocoupler trigger: writing LOW energizes the relay (turns it ON), while writing HIGH de-energizes it (turns it OFF). Multi-channel boards sometimes feature a jumper to select Active-HIGH or Active-LOW.

basics.title: COM, NO and NC contacts
basics.text: COM (Common) is the incoming power terminal. NO (Normally Open) connects to COM only when the relay is energized. NC (Normally Closed) connects to COM when the relay is OFF, and breaks the connection when energized.

basics.title: Coil current & USB limits
basics.text: Each 5V relay coil consumes about 70–80 mA when engaged. A single relay runs fine off the Nano 5V pin, but 4-channel or 8-channel relay boards will overload the Nano regulator and need a separate 5V power supply.

basics.title: Flyback diode protection
basics.text: When an inductor coil turns off, its collapsing magnetic field generates a destructive reverse voltage spike (flyback). Arduino relay breakout boards already include a diode across the coil plus an optocoupler and transistor to keep your Nano safe.

safety: Warning: Mains electricity (110V/230V AC) can cause fatal electric shocks and fires. Never touch terminal screws when connected to wall outlets. When learning, always stick to safe DC voltages (e.g. 5V, 12V or 24V batteries/adapters).

terminals.name: Common
terminals.meaning: The center terminal connected to the moving contact blade.
terminals.use: Connect this to the positive wire from your load's external power supply.

terminals.name: Normally Open
terminals.meaning: Disconnected from COM when the relay is unpowered; snaps shut to COM when energized.
terminals.use: Standard switch: device stays OFF until the Arduino turns the relay ON.

terminals.name: Normally Closed
terminals.meaning: Connected to COM when unpowered; breaks open when the relay is energized.
terminals.use: Fail-safe: device stays ON until Arduino turns relay ON (e.g. emergency shutoff or alarm).

jdVccGuide.title: The JD-VCC Jumper (Complete Opto-Isolation)
jdVccGuide.text: On 2/4/8-channel relay boards, there is a 3-pin jumper labelled VCC, JD-VCC, and GND. With the jumper in place, the relay coils draw 5V from the Arduino. If you remove the jumper, you can feed an independent 5V power supply to JD-VCC and GND, keeping the Arduino and coil power completely isolated from each other.

types.name: Electromechanical (EMR)
types.technology: Electromagnetic coil & mechanical spring contacts (e.g. Songle SRD-05VDC-SL-C)
types.isolation: Physical air gap (magnetic coil to contact arm)
types.looks: Classic blue rectangular plastic box with 5 pins on a breakout board with 3 screw terminals.
pros: Works with both AC and DC loads
Very low ON-resistance (no heat sinks needed for moderate currents)
Cheap and widely available in kits
cons: Cannot be switched with PWM (too slow)
uses: Turning on garden pumps and lights
Controlling garage doors and solenoid locks
types.note: The most common relay in beginner Arduino kits. Listen for the characteristic mechanical click when it switches.

types.name: Solid State Relay (SSR)
types.technology: Semiconductor optocoupler + Triac / MOSFET (e.g. Fotek SSR-25DA or Omron G3MB-202P)
types.isolation: Pure optical isolation (internal infrared LED & phototriac)
types.looks: Sleek black or grey block; hobby modules are often thin Omron G3MB modules on a red PCB.
pros: Fast switching, zero-cross switching suppresses electrical noise
cons: Triac types only switch AC loads, not DC
Slight voltage drop (~1–2V) generates heat under heavy loads
Small leakage current even when off
uses: PID temperature control for heating elements / 3D printer beds
Fast light flashing and stage effects
types.note: Standard Triac SSRs will NOT turn off on DC voltages! Use MOSFET SSRs for DC loads or stick to electromechanical relays.

types.name: Reed Relay
types.technology: Hermetically sealed glass capsule with flexible magnetic reeds inside an energizing coil
types.looks: Small dual-in-line (DIP) IC package or clear glass tube wrapped in thin copper wire.
pros: Extremely low coil current (often < 10 mA, can be driven directly by some MCU pins)
cons: Low current capacity (cannot run heavy motors or heaters)
uses: Audio signal switching and guitar pedals
types.note: Ideal for clean audio or measuring signals where you need mechanical contact without noisy SSR leakage.

types.name: Latching (Bistable) Relay
types.technology: Permanent magnet hold mechanism with dual set/reset coils or pulse-reversal coil
types.looks: Looks like a standard relay box, but usually marked 'Latching' or dual coil pins.
pros: Zero power consumption in steady state (only needs a 20 ms pulse to flip state)
cons: Requires dual-pulse or H-bridge driver circuit to switch directions
uses: Battery-powered IoT sensors and remote solar stations
types.note: The gold standard for low-power and battery setups where keeping a regular relay energized would drain the battery in hours.

types.name: MOSFET Switch Module
types.technology: Power N-Channel or P-Channel MOSFET (e.g. IRF520 or LR7843)
types.looks: Small PCB with a 3-pin TO-220 transistor with a metal tab or heatsink.
pros: Supports PWM for dimming DC LEDs and variable motor speed
types.note: Not technically a relay, but the best modern alternative whenever you need to switch or dim DC loads.

modules.name: 1-Channel 5V Relay Module
modules.purpose: The standard starter module with one Songle relay, status LED, flyback diode and transistor driver.
uses: Controlling a single 12V fan or lamp

modules.name: 2-Channel Optocoupled Relay Board
modules.purpose: Two independent relays with EL817 optocouplers and JD-VCC isolation jumper.

modules.name: 4-Channel Relay Board
modules.purpose: Four relays on one board. Requires external 5V power supply to avoid Nano USB resets.

modules.name: 1-Channel Solid State Relay (G3MB-202P)
modules.purpose: Silent, spark-free AC switching with resistive fuse protection.

modules.name: 3.3V Low-Level Relay Module
modules.purpose: Designed specifically for 3.3V microcontrollers like ESP32, ESP8266, and Raspberry Pi without level shifting.

examples.title: Active-LOW Relay Toggle (Every 3s)
examples.description: The fundamental sketch for standard Arduino relay breakout modules. Demonstrates the inverted logic: LOW turns the relay ON, HIGH turns it OFF.
parts: External 12V LED or Load with Power Supply
code: // Relay turns ON for 3 seconds, then OFF for 3 seconds.
// Most Arduino relay modules are Active-LOW:
const int RELAY_ON  = LOW;   // Energizes the coil
const int RELAY_OFF = HIGH;  // Releases the coil
// Set pin HIGH BEFORE pinMode to prevent a momentary trigger during boot
Serial.println(F("Turning relay ON (COM connected to NO)..."));

examples.title: Pushbutton Latch (Toggle Switch)
examples.description: Press a momentary pushbutton to toggle the relay between ON and OFF, with software debouncing. Useful for wall-switch replacements.
code: // Toggle Relay with Debounced Pushbutton (Internal Pullup)
Serial.println(F("Press the button to toggle the relay."));
// Trigger only on press down (falling edge)
